sections.figure_alt: A plant block with a gain returned and subtracted.
sections.body_md:
Pole placement asks you to name the closed-loop polynomial. A quadratic regulator asks you to name a cost, and it returns the gain that minimizes that cost. The infinite-horizon cost with constant weights produces a constant gain. There is one algebraic equation to solve, not a new gain at each time.

The state weight says which directions are expensive to leave large. The control weight says which commands are expensive to use. A larger control weight buys a smaller gain. A larger state weight buys a more aggressive one. Neither weight is a hard limit.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The cost is \(\int_0^{\infty} (x^T Q x + u^T R u)\, dt\), and the gain is \(K = R^{-1} B^T P\), where \(P\) solves
\[
A^T P + P A - P B R^{-1} B^T P + Q = 0.
\]
For the scalar integrator \(\dot{x} = u\) this collapses to \(K = \sqrt{q/r}\). For \(\dot{x} = a x + b u\) the scalar equation is a quadratic in \(P\), and the positive root is the one that stabilizes \(a - b K\) when the weights are positive and the pair is reachable. The negative root is not a cost matrix.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: For \(\dot{x} = u\) with state weight \(1.69\) and control weight \(0.25\), the gain is \(\sqrt{1.69/0.25} = \sqrt{6.76} = 2.6\). The Riccati solution itself is \(\sqrt{1.69 \times 0.25} = 0.65\), and dividing by the control weight recovers \(0.65/0.25 = 2.6\). Reporting \(0.65\) reports \(P\). Reporting \(6.76\) reports the ratio inside the square root, before the root is taken.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The comparative static on \(R\) runs backward if you think of a larger weight as permission to use more command. It is a penalty. The Riccati equation is not the Lyapunov equation: it carries the extra term that contains the gain, and deleting that term answers a stability question you were not asked. On a scalar plant it is also easy to return \(P\) when the question asked for \(K\), or to keep the negative root because it satisfies the same quadratic.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A hard bound on the command is not a large \(R\). The weight still allows every real number, and it only makes the large ones expensive. A finite horizon with the bound written as a constraint is the design that can mark those commands illegal. The same cost can also be written on a state that has already been augmented with an integrator. The gain then has one more entry, and the algebra is unchanged.
